title: Glow Recipe brand overview (public positioning) > Positioning
text:
Glow Recipe brand overview (public positioning) > Positioning

- **Tagline:** "Clinically Effective. Fruit-Powered. Glowing Skin."
- **Ingredient philosophy:** "gentle, yet effective formulas using the highest quality ingredients". Each product pairs "antioxidant-rich fruit with gentle yet powerful actives".

- **Education-led:** "At Glow Recipe, we want you to love & embrace your skin and that starts with learning about it!" The site's Glow 101 hub calls itself "your one-stop destination to learn about your skin".

title: Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook)
text:
Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook)

This policy applies to **all** customer-facing copy: ads, PDP copy, emails, SMS, social posts, influencer briefs, customer-care replies and AI-generated drafts.

**Severity levels**

- **BLOCK:** the copy must not ship. Rewrite it or escalate to Regulatory.
- **REVIEW:** the copy may ship only after Regulatory sign-off, recorded in the claims register (sop/ad-claim-review).
- **GUIDE:** a style requirement. The copy reviewer fixes it directly.

title: Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-01 No disease or treatment claims (BLOCK)
text:
Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-01 No disease or treatment claims (BLOCK)

Skincare products here are cosmetics. Copy may describe **appearance**. It must not describe treating, curing, healing or preventing a condition.
Source: compliance/fda-cosmetic-vs-drug.

Do not write: treats / cures / heals; Write instead: helps skin look / feel ....
Do not write: eczema, rosacea, psoriasis, dermatitis; Write instead: (do not name medical conditions).
Do not write: repairs your skin barrier; Write instead: supports a healthy-looking skin barrier.
Do not write: anti-inflammatory; Write instead: soothing, calming-feeling.
Do not write: regenerates cells, boosts collagen; Write instead: smoother, plumper-looking skin.

| treats / cures / heals | helps skin look / feel ... |

title: Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-02 BHA / salicylic acid products: no acne-treatment claims (BLOCK)
text:
Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-02 BHA / salicylic acid products: no acne-treatment claims (BLOCK)

Applies to: P482535 Strawberry Smooth BHA + AHA Salicylic Acid Serum, P504125 Strawberry BHA Pore-Smooth Blur Drops, P458219 / P467762 Watermelon Glow PHA + BHA Pore-Tight Toner.

- Do not write: "treats acne", "clears breakouts", "acne treatment", "gets rid of pimples", "prevents breakouts".
- Allowed: "helps unclog the look of pores", "smoother-looking texture", "for skin with visible pores".
- **Do not promise "no breakouts" or "won't break you out".** In research/insights-P482535, 24% of reviews mention breakouts or purging, and so do 47% of 1-2★ reviews. Recommend a patch test and gradual introduction.

title: Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-04 AHA products: sun-sensitivity disclosure (REVIEW)
text:
Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-04 AHA products: sun-sensitivity disclosure (REVIEW)

Applies to products with AHAs (compliance/fda-aha-labeling): P501254 / P501570 Watermelon Glow AHA Night Treatment, P436359 / P441323 Blueberry Bounce Gentle Cleanser, P482535 Strawberry Smooth serum, P469211 Pink Dream Body Cream.

- PDP, educational and routine content must include the FDA Sunburn Alert, or a link to it.
- Routine content featuring these products must show or mention **daily SPF**.

- AHA % and pH are **not** in the knowledge base. Do not state them.

title: Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-05 Sunscreen is an OTC drug (BLOCK)
text:
Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-05 Sunscreen is an OTC drug (BLOCK)

Applies to: P481989 Watermelon Glow Niacinamide Sunscreen SPF 50. Source: compliance/fda-sunscreen-labeling.

- Never use: "sunblock", "waterproof", "sweatproof".
- "Water resistant (40/80 minutes)" and "broad spectrum": only if the claims register holds the test result. The register has no such entry, so **REVIEW**.
- Do not write "all-day protection" or "no need to reapply". Any usage copy must say "reapply at least every 2 hours".
- Do not write **"no white cast"** or "invisible on all skin tones" as absolute claims. In research/insights-P481989, 26% of reviews mention white cast, with mixed sentiment.
- Do not write "won't pill under makeup". Pilling is the top complaint for this product: 68% of 1-2★ reviews mention it.

title: Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-07 Using customer reviews in marketing (REVIEW)
text:
Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-07 Using customer reviews in marketing (REVIEW)

Source: compliance/ftc-endorsement-guides, compliance/ftc-health-claims.

- Quote reviews **verbatim**. Keep the review_id so it can be traced.
- A quoted review becomes **our claim**. Rules CP-01 to CP-06 apply to the quote too. For example, "this cleared my acne" is blocked.
- Do not imply that one review's result is typical. Choose quotes that reflect the theme's real share in research/insights-* docs.
- Do not suppress or hide negative reviews. Do not offer incentives conditional on positive reviews.

title: Marketing claims policy (internal rulebook) > CP-09 "Clean", "natural" and "safe" language (BLOCK)
text:

- Never use: "chemical-free", "non-toxic", "toxin-free", "100% natural", "safe for everyone".

- **"Fragrance-free"** may be used only when the product's ingredient list has no fragrance/parfum. Most products contain fragrance (`actives: [fragrance]` in the product docs). Do not call those products suitable "for sensitive skin" without REVIEW.

title: Brand voice & copy guide > Four voice pillars
text:
Brand voice & copy guide > Four voice pillars

Pillar: **Joyful**; Means: Sensory, playful, fruit-forward; Sounds like: "a juicy hit of hydration", "dewy, bouncy skin"; Never sounds like: childish, all caps, more than 2 emojis per line.
Pillar: **Smart**; Means: Explain the active simply and name it; Sounds like: "PHA + BHA gently exfoliate to refine the look of pores"; Never sounds like: jargon without explanation, pseudo-science.
Pillar: **Honest**; Means: Set real expectations, admit trade-offs; Sounds like: "start 2-3 nights a week", "patch test first"; Never sounds like: "miracle", "instant results", "works for everyone".
Pillar: **Inclusive**; Means: All skin types and tones, no shame; Sounds like: "for every skin type in the Glow Gang"; Never sounds like: "fix your flaws", "bad skin", "problem skin".
display_text:
| Pillar | Means | Sounds like | Never sounds like |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Joyful** | Sensory, playful, fruit-forward | "a juicy hit of hydration", "dewy, bouncy skin" | childish, all caps, more than 2 emojis per line |
| **Smart** | Explain the active simply and name it | "PHA + BHA gently exfoliate to refine the look of pores" | jargon without explanation, pseudo-science |
| **Honest** | Set real expectations, admit trade-offs | "start 2-3 nights a week", "patch test first" | "miracle", "instant results", "works for everyone" |
| **Inclusive** | All skin types and tones, no shame | "for every skin type in the Glow Gang" | "fix your flaws", "bad skin", "problem skin" |

title: Brand voice & copy guide > Vocabulary
text:
Brand voice & copy guide > Vocabulary

**Use:** glow, dewy, juicy, bouncy, plump-looking, refined-looking pores, smooth-looking texture, Glow Gang, Glow-Tip, fruit-powered, gentle.

**Avoid (style):** flawless, perfect, flaws, anti-aging (say "fine lines"), hack, cheap, "holy grail" in brand voice (fine inside a quoted review).

**Banned (compliance):** see brand/claims-policy. Examples: cure, treat, acne treatment, whitening, chemical-free, non-toxic, sunblock, waterproof, clinically proven (without a study ID).

title: Brand voice & copy guide > Talking about scent
text:
Brand voice & copy guide > Talking about scent

Scent is one of the most-mentioned themes in reviews, and it divides people. Examples from research/insights-*:

- Watermelon Pink Juice Moisturizer: scent is mentioned in 58% of reviews and is "mixed" (P428819).
- Blueberry Bounce Cleanser: scent is mentioned in 51% of reviews and is "mixed" (P436359).

Rules:

- Describe the scent concretely ("fresh watermelon") but do not make it the only reason to buy.
- Never imply a fragranced product is fragrance-free or "for sensitive skin" (CP-09).

title: Brand voice & copy guide > Channel formats
text:
Brand voice & copy guide > Channel formats

Channel: Meta / TikTok ad primary text; Length: 1-3 short lines; Structure: hook, benefit, proof, CTA; Notes: proof = real review quote with review_id (CP-07) or ingredient fact.
Channel: Headline; Length: ≤ 40 characters; Structure: benefit-led; Notes: no claims requiring REVIEW unless approved.
Channel: Email subject; Length: ≤ 45 characters; Structure: curiosity or benefit; Notes: max 1 emoji.
Channel: PDP bullets; Length: 3-5 bullets; Structure: what it is, key actives, who it's for, how to use; Notes: include CP-04 / CP-05 disclosures where relevant.
Channel: Customer care reply; Length: 3-6 sentences; Structure: empathize, answer, next step; Notes: see sop/review-response.

title: FDA guidance: labeling for cosmetics containing alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) > The concern
text:
FDA guidance: labeling for cosmetics containing alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) > The concern

When AHAs are applied to the skin they can make it more sensitive to the sun. This lasts while the product is used and for up to a week after stopping, which can increase the chance of sunburn.

title: FDA guidance: labeling for cosmetics containing alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) > Recommended label statement (verbatim)
text:
FDA guidance: labeling for cosmetics containing alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) > Recommended label statement (verbatim)

title: FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Legal definitions (FD&C Act)
text:
FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Legal definitions (FD&C Act)

- **Cosmetic:** articles "intended to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled, or sprayed on ... the human body ... for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance."
- **Drug:** articles "intended for use in the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease" and articles "intended to affect the structure or any function of the body."

title: FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Intended use decides the category
text:
FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Intended use decides the category

FDA looks at three things to decide what a product is intended to do:

1. **Claims** in labeling, advertising, websites and social media. A therapeutic claim makes the product a drug, even if the formula is a normal cosmetic.
2. **Consumer perception**, meaning what the product's reputation leads people to expect.
3. **Ingredients** that are well known for a therapeutic use (for example fluoride in toothpaste).

3. **Ingredients** that are well known for a therapeutic use (for example fluoride in toothpaste).

title: FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Claims that make a product a drug
text:
FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Claims that make a product a drug

FDA's examples include claims to:

- "restore hair growth"
- "reduce cellulite"
- "treat varicose veins"
- "increase or decrease the production of melanin (pigment) in the skin"
- "regenerate cells"
- treat dandruff
- protect from the sun (sunscreen claims)
- treat acne

title: FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Products that are both
text:
FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Products that are both

Some products are both a cosmetic and a drug and must meet both sets of rules. FDA's examples: anti-dandruff shampoos, fluoride toothpastes, antiperspirant deodorants, and **moisturizers or makeup marketed with sun-protection claims**.

title: FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Why this matters for Glow Recipe products
text:
FDA: Is it a cosmetic, a drug, or both? > Why this matters for Glow Recipe products

These notes are the knowledge base's own reading of the rule, not FDA text:

- **Watermelon Glow Niacinamide Sunscreen SPF 50 (P481989)** has sun-protection claims, so it is an OTC drug. See brand/claims-policy rule CP-05.
- **Salicylic acid (BHA) products**, such as P482535, P504125 and P458219, are cosmetics only as long as the marketing does not claim to treat acne. See CP-02.
- **"Dark spot" and "brightening" language**, as in Guava Vitamin C Dark Spot Treatment Serum (P475543), must describe appearance ("the look of dark spots"). It must not claim to change melanin production. See CP-03.

title: MoCRA: serious adverse event reporting for cosmetics
text:
MoCRA: serious adverse event reporting for cosmetics

The Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022 (MoCRA) made adverse event reporting mandatory for cosmetics sold in the U.S.
display_text: The Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022 (MoCRA) made adverse event reporting mandatory for cosmetics sold in the U.S.

title: MoCRA: serious adverse event reporting for cosmetics > Reporting duty
text:
MoCRA: serious adverse event reporting for cosmetics > Reporting duty

- The **responsible person** (manufacturer, packer or distributor named on the label) must report **serious adverse events** linked to a cosmetic product to FDA **within 15 business days** of receiving the report.
- If new medical information arrives **within 1 year** of the first report, it must also be sent to FDA within 15 business days.
- FDA recommends submitting reports on **MedWatch Form 3500A**, either electronically or on paper.

- FDA recommends submitting reports on **MedWatch Form 3500A**, either electronically or on paper.

title: MoCRA: serious adverse event reporting for cosmetics > What counts as "serious"
text:
MoCRA: serious adverse event reporting for cosmetics > What counts as "serious"

A serious adverse event includes **significant disfigurement**, for example:

- serious and persistent rashes
- second- or third-degree burns
- significant hair loss
- persistent or significant change in appearance

A reaction also counts as serious if it needs **medical or surgical intervention** to prevent one of these outcomes. Reactions that are expected under normal use do not count.

title: FDA: OTC sunscreen labeling rules (21 CFR 201.327)
text:
FDA: OTC sunscreen labeling rules (21 CFR 201.327)

In the U.S., sunscreens are **over-the-counter (OTC) drugs**. Their labeling is governed by 21 CFR 201.327 (the 2011 labeling and effectiveness testing rule).
display_text: In the U.S., sunscreens are **over-the-counter (OTC) drugs**. Their labeling is governed by 21 CFR 201.327 (the 2011 labeling and effectiveness testing rule).

title: FDA: OTC sunscreen labeling rules (21 CFR 201.327) > Prohibited terms
text:
FDA: OTC sunscreen labeling rules (21 CFR 201.327) > Prohibited terms

The terms **"sunblock"**, **"sweatproof"** and **"waterproof"** are not allowed. Using them, or similar terms, makes the product misbranded under section 502 of the FD&C Act.
display_text: The terms **"sunblock"**, **"sweatproof"** and **"waterproof"** are not allowed. Using them, or similar terms, makes the product misbranded under section 502 of the FD&C Act.

title: FDA: OTC sunscreen labeling rules (21 CFR 201.327) > Water resistance
text:
FDA: OTC sunscreen labeling rules (21 CFR 201.327) > Water resistance

- A product can only claim water resistance if it passes the test in the regulation. The claim must then read **"Water Resistant (40 minutes)"** or **"Water Resistant (80 minutes)"**.
- Products that pass must tell users to reapply "after 40 [or 80] minutes of swimming or sweating", "immediately after towel drying" and "at least every 2 hours".
- Products that do **not** pass must say "reapply at least every 2 hours" and "use a water resistant sunscreen if swimming or sweating".

title: FDA: OTC sunscreen labeling rules (21 CFR 201.327) > Other points
text:
FDA: OTC sunscreen labeling rules (21 CFR 201.327) > Other points

- "Broad Spectrum" may only be claimed if the product passes the broad-spectrum test.
- The SPF value on the label must match test results.

title: FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > When a disclosure is required
text:
FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > When a disclosure is required

An influencer or endorser must disclose a **material connection** to the brand, meaning one "that a significant minority of consumers wouldn't expect and it would affect how they evaluate the endorsement." This includes:

- being paid to mention the product
- **receiving free product**, including PR boxes and gifted items
- an ongoing relationship such as affiliate commissions or ambassador programs. **Each post needs its own disclosure**, even if earlier posts already disclosed it.

- an ongoing relationship such as affiliate commissions or ambassador programs. **Each post needs its own disclosure**, even if earlier posts already disclosed it.

title: FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > How to disclose
text:
FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > How to disclose

- Simple and direct, for example "Ad", "Paid post" or "#ad", placed at the beginning.
- Hard to miss: visible without clicking "more", not hidden among hashtags, not only in the comments.
- In video, put the disclosure **in the video itself** (on-screen text and spoken), not only in the description.
- Not as a hyperlink.
- **Not adequate:** "#endorsed" (ambiguous), "#gifted" alone (does not say who gave it), or a platform's built-in label alone.

title: FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > Truthfulness
text:
FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > Truthfulness

Endorsers must:

- only describe experiences they actually had
- not misrepresent how often they use the product
- not make claims the brand could not substantiate
- give their honest opinion, which may include criticism

title: FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > Reviews
text:
FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > Reviews

Companies **must not**:

- ask only happy customers for reviews
- suppress or delay negative reviews while promoting positive ones
- make an incentive conditional on the review being positive
- display reviews in a misleading way (for example always showing 5★ first)

Incentivized reviews need a disclosure on each review. If incentives artificially raise ratings, the practice is still deceptive even with the disclosure.

title: FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > Brand responsibilities
text:
FTC Endorsement Guides: what people are asking > Brand responsibilities

Brands should run a reasonable **monitoring program**: train creators on allowed claims and on how to disclose, periodically check what they post, and act on non-compliance. FTC recommends pre-approving posts, especially for health or safety claims.

title: FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance
text:
FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance

Summary of the FTC guidance (December 2022), which replaced the 1998 dietary supplement guide. It covers advertising for health-related products. Skin-health and "clinical" claims for skincare fall under it.
display_text: Summary of the FTC guidance (December 2022), which replaced the 1998 dietary supplement guide. It covers advertising for health-related products. Skin-health and "clinical" claims for skincare fall under it.

title: FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 1. Every objective claim needs substantiation
text:
FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 1. Every objective claim needs substantiation

Health-related claims must be backed by **"competent and reliable scientific evidence"**: "tests, analyses, research, or studies that (1) have been conducted and evaluated in an objective manner by experts in the relevant disease, condition, or function to which the representation relates; and (2) are generally accepted in the profession to yield accurate and reliable results."

FTC treats randomized controlled human trials as the strongest evidence for health benefit claims.

Health-related claims must be backed by **"competent and reliable scientific evidence"**: "tests, analyses, research, or studies that (1) have been conducted and evaluated in an objective manner by experts in the relevant disease, condition, or function to which the representation relates; and (2) are generally accepted in the profession to yield accurate and reliable results."

FTC treats randomized controlled human trials as the strongest evidence for health benefit claims.

title: FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 2. Express and implied claims both count
text:
FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 2. Express and implied claims both count

Advertisers must substantiate claims stated directly **and** claims "suggested or reasonably implied" by the ad. What matters is how consumers understand the ad, not what the advertiser meant.
display_text: Advertisers must substantiate claims stated directly **and** claims "suggested or reasonably implied" by the ad. What matters is how consumers understand the ad, not what the advertiser meant.

title: FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 3. Net impression
text:
FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 3. Net impression

An ad is judged by its **"net impression"**: everything in it together, "including the text, product name, and any charts, graphs, and other images." For example, a product name or a before/after image can create a claim even if the copy never states it.

title: FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 4. Disclosures must be clear and conspicuous
text:
FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 4. Disclosures must be clear and conspicuous

If a claim needs qualifying information, the disclosure must be "easily noticeable" and "easily understandable by ordinary consumers." It must appear in the same format as the claim (on screen for visual claims, spoken for audio claims). Fine print alone is not enough. A disclosure cannot fix a claim that is false.

title: FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 5. Testimonials and endorsements
text:
FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > 5. Testimonials and endorsements

Advertisers are "liable for the misleading use of endorsements". A customer quote saying a product "cleared my acne" is a claim the brand must be able to substantiate. Material connections with endorsers must be disclosed (see compliance/ftc-endorsement-guides).

text:
FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance > Practical implications (knowledge base's reading)

- "Clinically proven", "dermatologist recommended", "visible results in 7 days" and similar claims need a study on file. The knowledge base contains **no clinical study data** for any product, so the assistant cannot confirm that such a claim is substantiated.
- Quoting a real review in an ad does not exempt the claim it contains. A review quote counts as the brand's own claim. See brand/claims-policy CP-07.

title: Creative brief template
text:
Creative brief template

Use this template for ads, creator briefs and campaign concepts. Every factual line needs a source: a product doc, a research/insights-* doc, a review_id or a policy rule. If a section cannot be filled from the knowledge base, write **"Unknown, not in knowledge base"**. Do not guess.

---

**1. Product:** name, product ID, price (from product/<id>)

**2. Objective:** awareness / acquisition / retention / education

**3. Audience:** who it is for (skin type, concern). Cite the skin-type segment from research/insights-<id>, and note any segment flagged "insufficient sample".

**4. Customer insight:** one sentence, with the theme %, and 1-2 verbatim quotes with review_id.

**5. Key message:** one line in brand voice (brand/voice-guide).

**6. Reasons to believe:** ingredients from the product doc, and the review theme share. No clinical claims unless the claims register approved them (CP-06).

**7. What we learned before:** relevant test IDs from creative/learnings-2023, or "no prior test".

**8. Mandatories:**
- disclosures: CP-04 Sunburn Alert, CP-05 reapply, CP-10 #ad
- the rule IDs that apply from the brand/claims-policy quick lookup

**9. Do not say:** product-specific banned phrases from brand/claims-policy.

**10. Format & channel:** for example a 15-30 second Reels/TikTok UGC video, with the hook in the first 2 seconds.

**11. Success metric:** primary metric and the threshold for a winner (creative/learnings-2023 "How to read this").

**12. Open risks / unknowns:** data gaps that affect this brief.

text:

title: Creative learnings, paid social (Q3 2022 to Q1 2023) > Cross-test learnings
text:
Creative learnings, paid social (Q3 2022 to Q1 2023) > Cross-test learnings

1. **Lead with the praise theme that customers actually use.** The three biggest CPA wins (CT-01, CT-05, CT-08) each led with the product's #1 praise theme from research/insights-*.
2. **Address the top complaint in education, not acquisition.** Complaint-led creative (CT-02, CT-03, CT-07) did not lower CPA. CT-03 did cut negative comments, so it is worth running as an always-on education ad.
3. **Compliance failures were all hook-level.** All three incidents (CT-04, CT-06 Hook B, CT-10) came from hooks or offers, not body copy. Run the claim check on hooks first (sop/ad-claim-review).
4. **UGC beat studio** in 3 of 3 head-to-head tests. Real application footage also lets us show pilling or white cast honestly instead of claiming they don't happen.

title: SOP: Ad & copy claim review > Steps
text:
SOP: Ad & copy claim review > Steps

1. **Self-check (copy owner).** Run the checklist below. Tag each product mentioned with its product ID.
2. **Classify.** If any BLOCK rule is hit, rewrite before submitting. If any REVIEW rule is hit, submit to Regulatory. If only GUIDE rules apply, submit to the copy reviewer.
3. **Submit** in the #claims-review channel with: copy, product IDs, channel, launch date, and the rule IDs it touches.
4. **SLA:**
   - GUIDE review: 1 business day.
   - REVIEW (Regulatory): 3 business days.
   - Paid social launches need approval at least **5 business days** before the flight date.
5. **Record.** Regulatory logs approved REVIEW claims in the **claims register** with the claim text, product ID, evidence or study ID, approver and expiry date (12 months).
6. **Post-launch.** If a live ad is found to break a BLOCK rule, pause it within 4 hours and log an incident.

- [ ] Creator posts open with #ad (CP-10).
- [ ] Price and shipping match product docs and policy/shipping (CP-11).

title: SOP: Adverse reaction escalation > Trigger
text:
SOP: Adverse reaction escalation > Trigger

Use this SOP when a customer tells us **directly**, by email, chat, DM or phone, that they had a reaction to a product. Reactions include burning, stinging, rash, swelling, blistering, eye irritation, or anything they saw a doctor for.

Public reviews on retailer sites are monitored separately (sop/review-response). If a public review describes a severe reaction, invite the customer to contact Care directly.

Use this SOP when a customer tells us **directly**, by email, chat, DM or phone, that they had a reaction to a product. Reactions include burning, stinging, rash, swelling, blistering, eye irritation, or anything they saw a doctor for.

Public reviews on retailer sites are monitored separately (sop/review-response). If a public review describes a severe reaction, invite the customer to contact Care directly.

title: SOP: Adverse reaction escalation > Steps
text:
SOP: Adverse reaction escalation > Steps

1. **Do not give medical advice.** Tell the customer to stop using the product and to seek medical care if symptoms are severe or getting worse.
2. **Collect within the same conversation:**
   - product name and product ID
   - batch or lot code from the pack
   - purchase channel (glowrecipe.com, Sephora, other)
   - date of first use and date of reaction
   - description of the reaction, and whether medical treatment was needed
   - photos, if the customer offers them
   - other products used at the same time
3. **Classify:**

Level: **Serious**; Definition: Matches the MoCRA definition: serious or persistent rash, 2nd/3rd-degree burn, significant hair loss, persistent change in appearance, or medical/surgical intervention needed; Action: Escalate to Regulatory **the same business day**. Regulatory files with FDA (MedWatch 3500A).; Deadline: FDA report within **15 business days** of receipt.
Level: **Non-serious**; Definition: Mild or temporary stinging, redness or breakouts with no medical care; Action: Log in the reaction tracker. Offer return or refund per policy/returns, or a goodwill gesture.; Deadline: Log within 1 business day.
Level: **Unclear**; Definition: Not enough information; Action: Ask follow-up questions and treat as **Serious** until classified; Deadline: same business day.

4. **Keep records** of all reports, serious or not.
5. **Follow up.** If new medical information arrives within 1 year of a serious report, send it to Regulatory. It must reach FDA within 15 business days.

title: SOP: Adverse reaction escalation > Do not
text:
SOP: Adverse reaction escalation > Do not

- Do not say "this is normal", "it's just purging" or "no one else has had this".

- Do not promise compensation in exchange for not reporting.

title: SOP: Writing an influencer / creator brief > When to use
text:
SOP: Writing an influencer / creator brief > When to use

Use this SOP for every paid, gifted or affiliate creator collaboration. Gifted PR boxes count too. Under the FTC Endorsement Guides, free product is a material connection (compliance/ftc-endorsement-guides).

title: SOP: Writing an influencer / creator brief > Steps
text:
SOP: Writing an influencer / creator brief > Steps

1. **Pick the product and angle.** Start from research/insights-<product_id>. Use a theme that customers actually praise (Leans = praise). Do not build the angle on a theme that mostly appears in complaints.
2. **Fill in creative/brief-template.**
3. **Add the product's mandatory rules** from the quick-lookup table in brand/claims-policy.
4. **Regulatory pre-approval** is required when the product has CP-02, CP-04, CP-05 or CP-08 rules, which cover BHA, AHA, sunscreen and retinol (sop/ad-claim-review).
5. **Send the brief, then review the draft post** before it goes live. Check disclosure, claims, and that the creator describes only their own experience.
6. **Monitor after posting.** Spot-check posts within 48 hours. If the disclosure is missing or a claim is blocked, ask for an edit within 24 hours. If the creator does not fix it, end the collaboration.

title: SOP: Writing an influencer / creator brief > Mandatory brief sections
text:
SOP: Writing an influencer / creator brief > Mandatory brief sections

- **Disclosure (CP-10):** "#ad" or "Ad" at the start of the caption **and** on screen in the first 3 seconds of video. "#gifted" alone is not acceptable. Repeat the disclosure in every post.
- **Honest experience:** the creator must use the product for at least 14 days before posting. They may mention downsides.
- **Do not say** (product-specific): copy from brand/claims-policy.
- **Must say** (product-specific): for example "reapply every 2 hours" for SPF, or "use SPF daily" for AHA and retinol products.

title: SOP: Responding to customer reviews & complaints > Principles
text:
SOP: Responding to customer reviews & complaints > Principles

1. **Never suppress, hide or delay a negative review.** Never ask a customer to change a rating in exchange for anything (compliance/ftc-endorsement-guides).
2. Respond to every 1-2★ review on owned channels within **2 business days**.
3. Respond in brand voice (brand/voice-guide): warm, honest, no blame.
4. **No medical advice.** Do not diagnose. Do not tell the customer a reaction is "just purging" or "normal".
5. Replies are customer-facing copy, so brand/claims-policy applies.

title: SOP: Responding to customer reviews & complaints > Triage
text:
SOP: Responding to customer reviews & complaints > Triage

Situation: Texture, scent, packaging, price or "didn't work for me"; Action: Reply with the template below. Offer usage tips. Mention the return policy only if the order is within policy..
Situation: Breakouts / "purging"; Action: Reply with the breakout template. Suggest stopping use and a patch test before reintroducing. No promises..
Situation: Burning, stinging, rash, swelling, or anything that needed a doctor; Action: **Stop.** Follow sop/adverse-event-escalation before replying..
Situation: Wrong item, damaged or missing package; Action: Create a care ticket. The return policy does not cover damaged items, so escalate to a Care lead..
Situation: Request for a refund outside 15 days, or an international order; Action: Explain the policy (policy/returns) and escalate to a Care lead for a goodwill decision. Do not promise an exception..

title: SOP: Responding to customer reviews & complaints > Reply templates
text:
SOP: Responding to customer reviews & complaints > Reply templates

**Generic "didn't work for me"**

> Hi {name}, thank you for sharing this, and we're sorry {product} wasn't the right match. {one usage tip relevant to the complaint}. If you ordered from glowrecipe.com within the last 15 days, email returns@glowrecipe.com and we'll send a free return label. 💧

**Pilling under makeup** (top complaint for P481989 sunscreen and present for P479327 moisturizer)

> Hi {name}, thanks for the honest feedback. Pilling can happen when layers don't have time to set. Many in our community wait 1-2 minutes before makeup and use a lighter layer underneath. We've shared your note with our product team.

**Breakouts**

> Hi {name}, we're sorry to hear that. Everyone's skin is different. We recommend pausing use and doing a patch test before trying again. If you have any discomfort, please reach out to care@... so we can help directly.

title: SOP: Responding to customer reviews & complaints > Usage tips by complaint theme
text:
SOP: Responding to customer reviews & complaints > Usage tips by complaint theme

These tips draw on what reviewers themselves report in research/insights-*. They are guidance, not claims.

- **Sticky feel** (Dew Drops P466123, Pink Juice P428819): use less product and let it absorb before the next layer.
- **Scent** (Pink Juice P428819, Blueberry P436359): be honest that the product is fragranced. Do not offer a "fragrance-free version", because none exists in the catalog.
- **Pilling** (Sunscreen P481989): see the template above.
